category_title: Artistically-inclined students who adapt storytelling skills to technical 3D modeling
minimal_context: The student is working in Cinema 4D to model 3D assets and adjust visual optics for a bike delivery game.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's look at your environment models for your bike delivery game in Cinema 4D. During the peer feedback session, it was mentioned that we need to work on the visual optics.

STUDENT: I got part of the idea for my game since my school is by Fisherman’s Wharf; I go there a lot. I just get to see the environment around there a lot so I know more about how it’s going to be.

TUTOR: That's good. How are you going to set up the models in the software?

STUDENT: I recreated San Francisco landmarks like Fisherman’s Wharf and the Golden Gate Bridge, but I'm having trouble trying to visualize three-dimensional objects in two-dimensional space.

TUTOR: What do you think you should try next to fix that?

STUDENT: I don't know what to do. A classmate made the observation that some of my early renderings were too flat. I know I'm supposed to use Cinema 4D's lighting tools to include shadows from both the bridge and bike to create a 3D effect, and play with depth of field, but the software is too complicated for me to figure out on my own.

options.A: Provide an anchored experience through a class visit to Fisherman's Wharf to take photos to use as visual prompts on a smartboard and iPad.
options.B: Utilize clear rubrics and maintain strict grading standards for the 3D assets while remaining available for student assistance requests during the 8-month course.
options.C: Calculate the final grade for the course as a combination of 30% from peer assessment and 70% from the final game project.
options.D: Break the modeling process down into phases, beginning by covering fundamental concepts such as three-dimensional space and representing objects using vertices and geometry.
